# Implement block: Loan Step Questions (Jetpack Compose)

You are adding the "Loan Step Questions" block from Native Cook to the user's Android app. The block already exists as working Kotlin code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A loan application on white, one question to a screen, in dark slate (#3A3F58) with royal blue (#3F5BD9) accents. "How much would you like to borrow?" stands in light 28 pt type over the label "Amount" and the figure "$25,000" at 80 pt light, its dollar sign pale grey; under it a ruler of fine lavender ticks moves beneath a blue marker fixed in the middle, with "1k" and "100k" at its ends, then a pale strip of two cells, "Monthly: $2,232" and, in blue, "Total: $26,781". A grey footer carries PREV and NEXT in blue capitals under a thin progress line. Dragging the ruler runs the figure, its changing digits ghosting, and both totals; NEXT sends the question, the label and the figure up and away with a vertical smear while "Over how many months would you like to repay?" and "12" rise from below, the ruler only dipping and trading its end labels for "6" and "96" and the progress line growing. A second NEXT takes the ruler and the totals away too and brings a summary: the monthly payment at the same giant size over two strips (amount, term, rate, total), with the right half of the footer turned into a blue CONFIRM bar.

**Motion.** The ruler has a tick every 10 pt (every fifth taller) and one tick is one step: $1,000 or one month. A drag pulls it under the marker, the figure following to a tenth of a tick ($100) for the amount and to the month for the months; past either end it follows 25% of the pull. On release it is thrown on by 0.16 s of the finger's speed and settles on the nearest tick with a spring (stiffness 190, damping 24, mass 1), a selection haptic at every tick. A digit that changes starts at 30% opacity and firms up in 260 ms (ease-out) while the digit it replaced fades from 40% under it; digits sit in cells of one width. A step change runs one value from 0 to 1 over 900 ms, linear. The leaving page's parts (question, label, figure, then ruler and totals when they leave too) start 12% apart, in that order, within the first 52%: each travels 70 pt up on u², its opacity falling with the distance and a vertical blur of up to 7 pt peaking half way. The coming page's parts start at 42% of the turn, staggered the same way, from 70 pt below on 1 − (1 − u)³. Going back plays it the other way up: the leaving page falls, the coming one descends. Between the two rulers the ruler stays: it dips 14 pt along one sine period (up, then back from below), slides to the other value's pull and cross-fades its end labels between 30% and 70% of the turn; the totals do not move. The progress line takes 500 ms (cubic ease-out) to reach a third per answered step and is full once confirmed; the NEXT half of the footer turns blue in 350 ms on the summary and reads SENT after a tap, with a success haptic. The self-playing demo shows a soft blue dot for the finger (56 pt, 16% blue): it drags the amount from $25,000 to $47,000 from 0.8 s over 1.4 s (cubic ease-in-out), taps NEXT at 2.6 s, drags the months from 12 to 29 from 3.8 s over 1.1 s, taps NEXT at 5.3 s, holds the summary and at 7.6 s goes back to the first question with the starting values, every 9.6 s, without haptics. A touch takes over, and 3 s later the loop returns to the first question and starts again. Under reduced motion parts only fade (no travel, no smear, no dip) in half the time and the ruler settles at once. The native ports follow the actual default-System timing code: under reduced motion the turn, digit ghosts, progress line and demo dot jump immediately, while the footer CSS transitions keep their durations. Automatic restart and dragging clear the retained manual haptic flag, and automatic confirmation suppresses success feedback, so every autoPlay path remains silent. SwiftUI approximates the strictly vertical smear with nine additive Gaussian samples; Compose uses native vertical-only blur on Android 12 and later, with a dim fallback on earlier Android. Native system-font paragraph and glyph metrics may differ from Skia; SwiftUI uses SF Symbols and Compose keeps the source icon outlines. Both guard missing question/label entries; Compose also guards nonpositive amount steps and unsupported narrow content widths.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [LoanStepQuestionsDemo.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/blocks/forms/loanstepquestions/LoanStepQuestionsDemo.kt)

### Files of the block

- [LoanStepQuestions.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/blocks/forms/loanstepquestions/LoanStepQuestions.kt)
- [Ruler.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/blocks/forms/loanstepquestions/Ruler.kt)

### Shared helpers the block uses

- [kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/shared/ComponentSupport.kt](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/kotlin/app/src/main/java/com/ngocdevv/nativecook/shared/ComponentSupport.kt)

### Libraries

It needs no library beyond a new Compose project.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced Android engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference on an emulator or a device. A Compose preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build, install and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and easing. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an Android app built with Gradle. If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app module, its namespace, `minSdk`, `compileSdk`, and the versions of Kotlin, the Android Gradle Plugin and Compose (a BOM or single versions).
- Whether Compose is switched on in that module, and whether screens are Compose, Views or both.
- Navigation: Navigation Compose, fragments, activities, or a single screen. Find how a screen is added today.
- How dependencies are declared: a version catalog (`libs.versions.toml`) or directly in `build.gradle`.
- Conventions: package layout, naming, theme, where resources live and how they are named.

### 3. Read the block

- Open the demo, then each file in the block's package. The list above names every file of the block, and the resources it uses from outside its package.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's parameters and their defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- Compare the block's libraries and the versions it was built with to the host's. Add what is missing the way this project declares dependencies. Do not upgrade the host's Kotlin, Gradle plugin or Compose versions without asking; if an API differs on the host's version, adapt the block's code.
- Check `minSdk`. If the block uses an API newer than the host's minimum, keep the fallback the source has, or tell the user what would be lost.
- If Compose is not switched on in the module, say what turning it on involves before you do it. In a View-based screen, show the block through a `ComposeView`.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block imports next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.

### 5. Bring it in

- Copy the block's files into a package of this app, and rewrite the `package` lines and the imports, including the import of the app's own `R` class.
- Copy its resources and asset files. Keep their names unless one collides with a resource of the app; then rename it everywhere it is used.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility descriptions as they are in the source. If the block needs a permission, add it to the manifest and say so.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen or destination named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build with the project's own task, for example `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug`, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Install and run it, and use the block: every state, every gesture, and once with animations switched off in the system settings.
- If the build or the emulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, dependencies and permissions added, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
